questions.question: What is the supreme law/rulebook of India called?
questions.explanation: The Constitution of India is the supreme legal document of the nation, laying down the fundamental governance framework, citizens' rights, and duties of the state.

questions.question: Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constitution?
questions.explanation: Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly, earning him the title of the Chief Architect of the Indian Constitution.

questions.question: Who was the Chairman of the Constituent Assembly?
questions.explanation: Dr. Rajendra Prasad presided as the permanent President/Chairman of the Constituent Assembly during its nearly three-year deliberative process, and later became India's first President.

questions.question: On what date was the Constitution formally adopted?
questions.explanation: The Constituent Assembly formally adopted and signed the completed Constitution on November 26, 1949—a day now celebrated nationwide as Constitution Day (Samvidhan Diwas).

questions.question: On what date did the Constitution come into effect (Republic Day)?
questions.explanation: The Constitution officially came into legal effect across India on January 26, 1950, marking India's birth as a sovereign Republic (celebrated annually as Republic Day).

questions.question: What is the introduction to the Constitution called?
questions.explanation: The Preamble is the introductory statement of the Constitution that articulates the core philosophy, guiding values, and ultimate aspirations of the Indian Republic.

questions.question: What rights are guaranteed to all citizens by the Constitution?
questions.explanation: Part III of the Constitution guarantees basic Fundamental Rights (such as equality, freedom, and protection against exploitation) to all citizens, enforceable by courts.

questions.question: Which part of the Constitution outlines the moral obligations of citizens?
questions.explanation: Part IV-A (Article 51A) enumerates the Fundamental Duties of Indian citizens, urging them to respect national symbols, cherish constitutional ideals, and protect public property.

questions.question: The word 'Secular' in the Preamble means the state has:
questions.explanation: In the Indian constitutional context, 'Secular' means the state has no official state religion, treats all religious faiths with equal respect (Sarva Dharma Sambhava), and grants citizens freedom of worship.

questions.question: Which document is kept safe in a helium-filled glass case in Parliament?
questions.explanation: The original calligraphed and illustrated copies of the Indian Constitution (in Hindi and English) are preserved inside special helium-filled glass cases in the Library of the Parliament of India.

questions.question: Why did India need a Constituent Assembly from diverse backgrounds?

options.text: Ensure all regions had a voice

questions.explanation: Including members from diverse regions, religions, castes, languages, and professions ensured that the Constitution reflected the collective will and aspirations of all segments of Indian society.

questions.question: What does it mean that the Constitution is a "living document"?

options.text: Can be amended to adapt to new times

questions.explanation: A living document can be amended and updated by Parliament (under Article 368) to meet changing societal needs, evolving democratic standards, and unforeseen future challenges.

questions.question: What is the difference between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles?
questions.explanation: Fundamental Rights are justiciable (enforceable in courts if violated), whereas Directive Principles of State Policy are non-justiciable moral guidelines instructing the state to build a welfare society.

questions.question: What does the term 'Republic' mean in the Preamble?

options.text: Head of state is elected, not hereditary

questions.explanation: A 'Republic' means the supreme Head of the State (the President of India) is elected directly or indirectly by the people for a fixed term, abolishing hereditary kingship.

questions.question: Why is the Constitution considered a shield against the misuse of power?
questions.explanation: By strictly delimiting powers across executive, legislative, and judicial branches and establishing fundamental citizens' rights, the Constitution prevents arbitrary or dictatorial state action.

questions.question: How did the Indian freedom struggle influence the Constitution?

options.text: Values like equality became the core

questions.explanation: Decades of anti-colonial struggle against British oppression inspired core constitutional values: liberty, racial/social equality, social justice, and self-governance.

questions.question: What does 'Sovereign' mean in the context of India?
questions.explanation: 'Sovereign' signifies that India is an completely independent nation possessing absolute internal and external authority, free from control or dictation by any foreign power.

questions.question: Why did India adopt Universal Adult Franchise immediately?
questions.explanation: Demonstrating profound faith in the wisdom of common citizens, the framers granted instant universal suffrage to every adult, rejecting colonial restrictions based on property or education.

questions.question: What role does the Judiciary play regarding the Constitution?

options.text: Guardian, ensuring laws don't violate it

questions.explanation: The Supreme Court acts as the ultimate constitutional custodian and interpreter, possessing the power of judicial review to strike down any legislative or executive act violating constitutional tenets.

questions.question: How many members were in the Constituent Assembly after Partition?
questions.explanation: Following the Partition of India in August 1947, the membership of the Constituent Assembly representing independent India settled at exactly 299 members.

questions.question: How does the Constitution balance majority rule with minority protection?
questions.explanation: While democratic decisions reflect majority votes, the Constitution protects religious and linguistic minorities through non-negotiable Fundamental Rights (like Articles 29 and 30) that no majority can abolish.

questions.question: Why is Dr. B.R. Ambedkar considered the "Chief Architect"?

options.text: Synthesized diverse ideas into a framework

questions.explanation: As Chairman of the Drafting Committee, Dr. Ambedkar masterfully synthesized vast comparative legal knowledge, debated complex clauses, and championed social justice, shaping the document's definitive architecture.

questions.question: What is the philosophical significance of "We, the People"?
questions.explanation: The opening words 'We, the People of India' affirm the doctrine of popular sovereignty: the Constitution derives its ultimate moral and legal legitimacy directly from the citizens of India.

questions.question: How do Fundamental Duties complement Fundamental Rights?

options.text: Remind citizens of responsibility to nation

questions.explanation: Rights and duties are two sides of the same democratic coin; Fundamental Duties remind citizens that enjoying liberties requires active civic responsibility toward community harmony and nation-building.

questions.question: Why was it crucial to implement 'Equality before Law' in India?
questions.explanation: In a society historically stratified by rigid caste hierarchies, untouchability, and gender bias, Article 14 ('Equality before Law') legally dismantled privilege and established universal legal parity.

questions.question: In what way did 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' influence the Constitution?
questions.explanation: The ancient Indian ideal 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' (the world is one family) inspired the constitutional pursuit of fraternity, international peace, and harmonious coexistence across diverse cultures.

questions.question: What would be the consequence if the Constitution could NOT be amended?
questions.explanation: An unamendable constitution would rigidify laws, making the state incapable of adapting to technological breakthroughs, social evolution, or crises, eventually leading to societal rupture.

questions.question: How does the separation of powers into three tiers aid governance?
questions.explanation: Decentralizing governance across Union, State, and Local (Panchayati Raj/Municipality) levels ensures grassroots participation, localized administrative efficiency, and responsive democratic delivery.

questions.question: Why is it said that without a Constitution, society might revert to 'Matsya Nyaya'?

options.text: The strong would consume the weak

questions.explanation: In ancient political philosophy, 'Matsya Nyaya' (law of the fish) describes a lawless state of nature where big fish devour small fish; the Constitution prevents this by restraining the powerful and protecting the weak.

questions.question: What does the 1992 amendment adding the Panchayati Raj signify?
questions.explanation: The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (1992) institutionalized Panchayats and Municipalities, deepening democracy by empowering village councils and reserving one-third of seats for women.
